memory_update.text: New Hotspots should be treated as a cross-sector chokepoint funnel rather than a single industry theme; AI infrastructure, critical minerals, sulphuric acid, grid power, and nuclear fuel are linked by demand shocks plus policy-constrained supply.
Indium phosphide optical substrates are a priority node because provided evidence indicates concentrated wafer supply, China-linked raw indium exposure, and export-permit friction.
HBM second-order suppliers remain relevant but require discipline because provided evidence says the producer layer and much of the direct supplier layer may already be recognized by the market.
Sulphur and sulphuric-acid feedstock should be tracked as a non-obvious bottleneck connecting copper, nickel HPAL, fertilizers, and global trade-route disruption.

AI data-center power interconnection should be split into obvious leaders and underfollowed component suppliers such as transformers, switchgear, busways, power monitoring, and grid construction subcontractors.
Later layers must verify all hotspot claims with primary filings, official policy documents, customer disclosures, market-cap data, and analyst-coverage checks before selecting candidates.

summary: Initial Serenity Layer 1A decomposition for emerging, underfollowed supply-chain hotspots. The strongest early hotspot clusters from the provided evidence are: AI optical substrate bottlenecks around indium phosphide and indium export controls; HBM and advanced-packaging second-order suppliers; sulphur and sulphuric-acid disruption feeding copper, nickel HPAL, and fertilizers; AI data-center power and grid capacity; nuclear fuel and regulated baseload power; and policy-driven critical-mineral rerouting. This is not a stock recommendation layer. The objective is to identify scarce nodes, demand shocks, policy chokepoints, and underfollowed public-market search lanes for later evidence work.

Provided evidence states that global InP wafer production is highly concentrated and that China controls a large share of refined indium supply.

theme_map.public_market_search_strategy: Use a two-lane funnel. First, map reference leaders to validate the demand shock: NVIDIA, AMD, Broadcom, TSMC, ASML, Arista, Vertiv, Eaton, Constellation, Cameco, Centrus, BWX Technologies, GE Vernova, Quanta Services, and hyperscalers. Second, deliberately search one or two layers beneath them for narrow suppliers with lower analyst attention: specialty substrates, optical wafers, HBM materials and process-control tools, sulphuric-acid logistics and smelter-acid byproduct suppliers, grid component makers, transformer and switchgear suppliers, nuclear fuel-cycle services, EPC subcontractors, and critical-mineral processors. Prefer public companies with plausible USD 300M-10B market caps where exposure is meaningful, while using larger names only as reference or when exposure is unusually pure.
supply_side_constraints: Indium phosphide wafer production appears highly concentrated, with refined indium supply and export permits acting as upstream constraints
HBM producers are already widely recognized, so the discovery edge likely shifts one or two layers down into sub-$50B suppliers, specialty equipment, materials, and packaging inputs
China's sulphuric-acid export ban and Russia's sulphur export restrictions, per provided Kpler context, create feedstock shortages affecting copper, nickel, and fertilizer chains
AI data centers face electrical interconnection, transformer, switchgear, backup power, thermal, permitting, and grid construction constraints
Nuclear and SMR supply chains depend on regulated fuel, HALEU enrichment, reactor components, licensing, and EPC execution capacity
Export licensing, environmental permitting, qualification cycles, and customer certification can matter as much as nominal production capacity
